sections.h2: Does Arkansas charge an estate tax when someone dies?
sections.html:
No. The Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration says the state estate tax was repealed by Act 645 of 2003, and that no Arkansas estate tax return is required for anyone who died after December 31, 2004.

For an heir holding a house, that settles the first worry. The state does not take a share of the estate based on its size, and there is no Arkansas return to file for the estate tax itself. DFA's one-page notice, revised in December 2020, is the source for this, and it is worth printing for the probate file if a title company or lender asks.

The notice speaks only to the estate tax. We could not open an official Arkansas page that addresses a separate inheritance tax, so this guide does not make a claim either way. An heir with a large inheritance can ask DFA or a probate attorney to confirm before distribution.

sections.h2: What about the federal estate tax?
sections.html:
The federal tax reaches only very large estates. The IRS states that a return is required when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, is above the filing threshold for the year of death, and that threshold is $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

The IRS adds that most relatively simple estates do not need to file. When one does, the IRS says the gross estate is valued at fair market value on the date of death, and deductions can include mortgages and other debts, estate administration expenses, property that passes to a surviving spouse and qualified charities. A surviving spouse may also elect to carry over the decedent's unused exemption, known as portability, on a timely filed return.

sections.h2: What income tax can an heir owe on selling an inherited Arkansas house?
sections.html:
Often very little, because the heir's basis usually starts at the home's value when the owner died. IRS Publication 551 lists the fair market value on the date of death as the basis of inherited property, or the value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elects it. It adds that heirs who receive a Schedule A (Form 8971) generally use the estate tax value reported there.

Gain is measured from that starting figure to the sale price. If the house sells for about its date-of-death value, the taxable gain tends to be small. If it rises in value while the heir waits, the increase is the gain. Arkansas then taxes only half of a net long-term gain, as explained in our guide to Arkansas capital gains tax on a house sale.

Income earned by the estate itself, such as rent collected before the sale, is a separate matter. DFA keeps a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms for personal representatives.

sections.h2: When can an Arkansas heir skip formal probate?
sections.html:
When the estate is small. Ark. Code 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and distribute estate assets without a personal representative if the property owned at death, less encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000. The decedent's homestead and any statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children are left out of that count.

That exclusion helps with houses. A family home that was the decedent's homestead does not eat into the $100,000 limit, though it still appears in the affidavit.

  • At least 45 days must have passed since the death.
  • No petition for appointment of a personal representative can be pending or granted.
  • One or more distributees file an affidavit with the probate clerk of the circuit court in the proper county.
  • The affidavit states that there are no unpaid claims, and that the Department of Human Services either furnished no benefits or has been reimbursed.
  • It lists personal property with values, and real property by legal description with value, including the homestead.
  • The clerk charges $25 to file and $5 per certified copy, and no extra fee applies if a will is attached.

sections.h2: What extra steps apply when the small estate includes real property?
sections.html:
The distributee must publish a notice of the death and the affidavit within 30 days after filing. The notice gives creditors three months from the first publication to present verified claims, and late claims are barred.

That three-month window is the practical timeline for an heir who wants to sell. A buyer or title company may want to see that the affidavit was filed, the notice ran and the claims period passed before a deed is signed. The statute also allows the distributee to open a bank account in the estate's name without a petition or court order, which is handy for holding sale proceeds and paying the last bills.

Estates over the limit, or with a dispute among heirs, go through a regular administration in the circuit court's probate division. That route has its own filings, and a probate attorney can explain which one fits.

sections.h2: What costs come with transferring or selling the house?
sections.html:
The main closing cost the state adds is the real property transfer tax. DFA says it is $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on a deed or instrument conveying realty, on transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 splits it into $1.10 per $1,000 and an added $2.20 per $1,000 that the statute says the purchaser pays.

Property tax is the other bill that follows the house. Under Ark. Code 26-36-201, real property tax is payable to the county collector from the first business day of March through October 15, taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent, and a 10% penalty applies. An estate that is still settling in the fall should check that the current year's bill has not slipped.

Utilities, insurance and upkeep continue until the deed is recorded, so a vacant inherited house can run up costs even when no tax is due on the estate.

sections.h2: What should heirs do first with an inherited Arkansas house?
sections.html:
Start by confirming who legally owns it and what has to be filed, then decide whether to keep, rent or sell.

  • Locate the will, the deed and the latest property tax statement.
  • Ask the county assessor or collector for the parcel's tax status.
  • Check whether the estate qualifies for the small estate affidavit, or needs a personal representative.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing, since it sets the basis for any later sale.
  • Secure the house and keep insurance active.
  • Speak with a probate attorney and a tax professional before signing a sale contract.

Heirs who live out of state, or who inherited a house needing repairs, sometimes choose a cash sale to avoid carrying costs and repair projects. The right choice depends on the estate's papers and the family's timeline.

faqs.q: Is there an Arkansas estate tax?
faqs.a: No. DFA says Act 645 of 2003 repealed the Arkansas estate tax, and no estate tax return is required for decedents who died after December 31, 2004.

faqs.q: Do heirs pay Arkansas inheritance tax on a house?
faqs.a: We could not confirm an Arkansas inheritance tax from an official page, so we make no claim. Ask DFA or a probate attorney, who can answer for your situation.

faqs.q: At what size does the federal estate tax apply?
faqs.a: A federal return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption exceeds the filing threshold for the year of death. The IRS lists it as $15,000,000 for 2026.

faqs.q: What is the Arkansas small estate limit?
faqs.a: Under Ark. Code 28-41-101, property owned at death, less encumbrances, can be up to $100,000, not counting the homestead and statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children. At least 45 days must pass after death.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have if real property is in a small estate?
faqs.a: Three months from the first publication of the notice. The notice must be published within 30 days after the affidavit is filed, and claims not presented in time are barred.

faqs.q: Will I owe tax if I sell an inherited house right away?
faqs.a: Usually little, since the basis is the fair market value at the date of death, per IRS Publication 551. The gain is the sale price minus that figure, and Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.
